In a video statement released on Monday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said forming a unity government was an "absolute necessity".

"You cannot form a government with Hamas supporters," he added. "You cannot fight Iran and the rest of its followers within extremist Islam if, inside the government, you rely on supporters of extremist Islam."

"It is only natural that the largest party should lead this government," he said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Nearly 80 percent of Britons see Israel as a threat to world peace
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Nearly 80 percent of Britons see Israel as a threat to world peace
Nearly four in five Britons see Israel as a serious threat to world peace, according to a survey published last week by the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen).
The figure rose from 48 percent in 2005 to 78 percent this spring, two-and-a-half years into the genocide in Gaza and just after Israel and the US had attacked Iran.
In July, a YouGov opinion poll commissioned by the Council for British-Arab Understanding found that only 17 percent of the British population believes that Israel is not committing genocide in Gaza.
The war on Iran has hit the UK economy, leaving households paying more for energy, food and mortgages. The rising bills have brought the cost of Israel’s wars in the Middle East home to British households.
Last week, the Bank of England raised its base rate from 3.75 percent to 4 percent, its first increase in more than three years. The rise pushes up payments for borrowers on mortgages and adds to the cost of taking out or renewing a home loan.

data.title: Middle East Eye: As heavy rains swamp Gaza's tents, Israel must face sanctions
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
As heavy rains swamp Gaza's tents, Israel must face sanctions
It took a mere dozen hours of the first winter storm to flood around 70,000 tents in Gaza. Even 1,000 would be worthy of major humanitarian action, but just imagine that multiplied by 70.
These devastating floods were predicted and predictable. Nothing about this should surprise anyone who has paid even the scantest attention to the humanitarian situation in Gaza.
Every year, Palestinians in the coastal enclave face the threat of flooding due to winter rains. Years ago, it was already challenging enough, as raw sewage flooded the streets, fuelling the spread of disease.
Israel’s blockade of Gaza, in place for two decades, along with periodic military bombardments, would render these inundations particularly life-threatening. Much of the debate in years past was about the inability to pump water out, including the lack of fuel for pumps, owing to Israel’s blockade.
In contrast to the situation in 2026, however, that was a minor crisis.

The policy, spearheaded by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu between 2011 and 2023, involved Qatari officials transferring tens of millions of US dollars in cash to the Gaza Strip in an effort to maintain stable relations between Israel and Hamas.
The investigation describes a process in which Israeli government and security officials asked Qatar to transfer the funds, while senior military officers reportedly received expensive gifts from Doha.
According to the report, the close connections between Qatar and Israel over Gaza were first discussed in 2011, during a secret meeting organised by then French President Nicolas Sarkozy.
Netanyahu and his Qatari counterpart Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani met at the Presidential Palace in Paris, where Al Thani offered his country's help in negotiating the release of Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit, who had been held captive by Hamas since 2006.
During the meeting, Al Thani also offered to transfer building materials, including cement and iron, to help rebuild the Palestinian enclave destroyed by Israeli bombardment.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Why are the UAE, Sudan and Egypt fighting for influence inside Ethiopia’s Tigray state?
data.author: Daniel Tester
data.summary:
Why are the UAE, Sudan and Egypt fighting for influence inside Ethiopia’s Tigray state?
Submitted by
Daniel Tester
on

Gulf kingdoms and neighbouring countries are transforming the crisis into a wider battle for the Horn of Africa
An Ethiopian Federal Police patrol on 9 October 2026 after forces pushed back the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) in Mekelle (AFP)
On
Fighting has continued across the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia, after a coalition of rebel groups seized territory in September.
The government, which the insurgents have vowed to overthrow, has managed to contain much of the fighting, although explosions were heard in Addis Ababa in October.
Tigray is no stranger to conflict. Amid accusations of war crimes and genocide, hundreds of thousands of people were killed and millions more displaced during the civil war from 2020-22.
But now there are fears that the current conflict could escalate into a war between Ethiopia and neighbouring Eritrea, which it accuses of backing the rebels. The two countries severed relations in October.
The Red Sea region is already beset with war across Sudan, Yemen and Somalia.
Ethiopia has an ally in the UAE, while Eritrea can look to Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Sudan for support.
Here’s everything you need to know about Tigray, past conflicts, and the role other countries are playing.
Where is Tigray?
Tigray is Ethiopia’s northernmost state, bordering Eritrea and a small part of Sudan.
Roughly the size of Slovakia or the US state of West Virginia, it has a population of around 7.5 million people, according to the Ethiopian government.
The majority of the inhabitants are Tigrayan, one of the 80-plus ethnic groups in Ethiopia and make up around six percent of the overall population.
The landscape is dominated by rocky highlands, which contain some of Ethiopia’s largest deposits of gold and other minerals.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Anti-Muslim influence campaign targeting UK traced back to Israel
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Anti-Muslim influence campaign targeting UK traced back to Israel
A new investigation has traced a major anti-Muslim propaganda campaign targeting Britain back to Israel.
The campaign, uncovered by academics Marc Owen Jones and Sohan Dsouza, was at its height before the UK's 2024 general election and the anti-Muslim riots that raged across the country later that year.
It involved large numbers of paid advertisements warning of an Islamic takeover of Britain masterminded by Qatar.
"Between 2024 and 2026, our investigation recorded more than 154m exposures to its British-targeted material," Jones and Dsouza wrote in an article published by The Nerve.
"Its first wave of British advertising ran in the months before the 2024 general election. The ads were also hammering the UK in the winter and spring leading up to the anti-Muslim riots that followed the Southport murders."

Iran’s IRGC says two oil tankers catch fire in Strait of Hormuz
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says fires broke out aboard two oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz after they took a route Tehran considers unauthorised.
“One of these vessels, a supertanker, hit a naval mine and exploded, and the second tanker, which was under the protection of the US aggressor’s fighter jets and was attempting to secretly pass through the illegal route, had an accident and was stopped in its place with a terrible fire,” the IRGC said in a statement carried by Iranian state television.
The IRGC repeated its warning that “the unauthorised route is unsafe and all ships cooperating with the terrorist and aggressive US army that intend to pass through this route will suffer this fate”.
